Employers increasingly use AI tools to screen CVs, rank candidates and assess applicants, and these tools process personal data covered by Kenya’s 

Data Protection Act, 2019. Section 35 gives a person the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, where the decision has legal effects or significantly affects them, subject to exceptions for contract necessity, authorising law with safeguards, and consent. 

Where such a decision is made, the person must be notified in writing and can ask for it to be reconsidered or for a new decision not based solely on automated processing. Regulation 22 of the Data Protection (General) Regulations, 2021 also requires meaningful information about the logic involved, an explanation of the likely consequences, steps to address bias, and human intervention. 

Employers and HR teams should review whether their hiring tools decide without human involvement and what applicants are told, and applicants should know they can ask for a decision to be reconsidered.

Your LLM can read 1 million tokens. So why does it still get your own documents wrong?

I have spent the last few months building RAG systems and multi-agent workflows in Django and Python, and the pattern keeps repeating: the model is rarely the problem. The document is.

Real business documents are messy. A policy PDF that references a spreadsheet. A contract with the key clause buried in an appendix. A CV where the most important experience is implied, never stated. Feed all of that into a long context window and the model will still miss things — not because it cannot read, but because it cannot tell what matters.

Three things I have learned the hard way:

1. Retrieval beats length. A well-chunked, well-ranked retrieval layer over 50 pages outperforms a raw 500-page dump every time. Relevance is a design decision, not a token count.

2. Structure is a feature. Headings, tables, dates, versions — when you preserve them instead of flattening a document into plain text, the model reasons far better.

3. The last mile is verification. Every generated answer that touches a real decision needs a trace back to the source passage. If a hiring manager or a customer cannot check where an answer came from, they should not trust it.

Long context is a wonderful capability. But treating it as a substitute for good retrieval, clean structure and verification is how teams ship impressive demos and unreliable products.

For the leaders here — CEOs, Directors, HR heads — when you evaluate an AI tool for your team, what do you look for first: the size of the context window, or proof that its answers can be traced back to your own documents?

On November 4, Stanford University hosted Samir Kaul, Founding Partner at Khosla Ventures, and our CEO Alfia Ilicheva for a fireside chat with students from the university's undergraduate, graduate and PhD programs. The conversation covered how to build resilient businesses in the age of AI, the difficult choices leaders are making about AI in their organizations, and what those decisions mean for the future of financial services.

Alfia described how Formulary has fully embraced the bionic future in fund administration, where AI takes on the operational work and frees up domain experts to deliver personalized advice and strategic partnership to clients. Judgment calls, decisions and final recommendations stay with humans, and accountants stand behind every number investors receive.

Drawing on his long career investing in some of the most successful AI-first companies, Samir shared lessons for building and growing a business in this new paradigm:

1. Find customers you can grow with. As AI makes products easier to build, trust becomes a bigger part of what sets a company apart. Can a small contract grow into a large one? Will the customer be patient with the mistakes a young company is bound to make? Does this customer look like the ones who will come next?

2. Let revenue follow the product. Whether a young company books $2 million or $8 million in a year matters far less than whether it can keep growing for a long time with healthy margins. A product sold half-finished tends to stay that way.

3. Know whose advice to take. One of the most important things a leader can learn is to separate the signal from the noise. 

4. Hard days count far more than credentials do. The AI era will reward resilience over pedigree. Founders who have never had a bad day tend to struggle when the first one inevitably comes.

5. Look outside your own department. Some of the biggest untapped opportunities in AI are in domains where the hard problems go beyond software. No one builds a startup alone. A CS major interested in energy could team up with someone studying physics or chemical engineering.

A survey by Mckinsey on the State of AI - yielded some startling revelations.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗜 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗗𝗨𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗜𝗧𝗬 𝗣𝗔𝗥𝗔𝗗𝗢𝗫

McKinsey's State of AI 2026 reveals a striking disconnect:
  • 80% report improved individual productivity from AI.
  • 37% report a positive enterprise-level EBIT contribution.

These are shares of survey respondents, not measured percentage increases in productivity or profit.

The takeaway? AI is making employees more productive. But translating those improvements into enterprise profitability remains a challenge.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 ₹𝟮.𝟭𝟲 𝗖𝗥𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝗤𝗨𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡
Consider a hypothetical IT services team:
• Size: 30 engineers
• AI Productivity Gain: 10 hours saved per person per week
• Annual Capacity Released: 14,400 hours (48 working weeks)
• Avg Internal Cost: ₹1,500 per hour
• Theoretical Capacity Value: ₹2.16 crore annually

Great on a presentation. But here's the catch.
If all 30 engineers remain on the team's payroll, contract revenue stays unchanged, and no additional business gets delivered...

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 ₹𝟮.𝟭𝟲 𝗰𝗿𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗣&𝗟?
It isn't there. At least, not yet.
Created capacity is not created financial value.
⠀
𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗡 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗗𝗨𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗜𝗧𝗬 𝗕𝗘𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗙𝗜𝗧?
Economic benefit becomes tangible when capacity is utilized into measurable outcomes:
→ Profitable Growth: Deliver additional work without increasing headcount.
→ Cost Optimization: Avoid planned hiring and eliminate preventable operating costs.
→ Revenue Acceleration: Bring revenue-generating products to market faster.
→ Margin Improvement: Reduce rework and strengthen delivery profitability.
⠀
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗟𝗘𝗔𝗗𝗘𝗥𝗦𝗛𝗜𝗣 𝗜𝗠𝗣𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘: 𝟯 𝗔𝗜 𝗥𝗢𝗜 𝗦𝗖𝗢𝗥𝗘𝗖𝗔𝗥𝗗𝗦

    How many productive hours or FTE-equivalent capacity have AI initiatives freed?
2. FINANCIAL Value Realized
     What measurable net cost savings or margin improvements have reached the P&L?
3. BUSINESS Value Created
    What incremental revenue, faster time-to-market, or measurable customer outcomes have we enabled?
Combining these measures into a single savings figure risks overstating AI ROI.
⠀

US GAAP, IFRS, and local reporting requirements often sit in the same team. Professionals who can move between them and explain the differences stand out quickly.

3. Skills over job titles
GCC hiring is moving towards skills-first evaluation. Specific, demonstrable experience in SEC filings, consolidation, or SOX control ownership carries more weight than a title alone.

4. Leadership readiness
GCC talent reports flag a leadership readiness gap. Reviewing a team's work and presenting to a CFO in another time zone is a different capability from doing the technical work well.

5. Comfort with automation and AI
Finance teams are expected to cut manual effort and verify AI-assisted output. A measurable process improvement on your record is a real advantage.

The takeaway

If you are a finance professional targeting these roles, build evidence of all five, not just the credentials.

Most HK tech candidates I screen ask for a 15-20% increase on their next move. In data and AI, I hear numbers well above that, and they tend to say them without blinking.

Recently I spoke with an engineer on a secondment contract who gave me his number in the first two minutes. He knew his monthly base, he knew his gratuity would be released at the end of the term, and he knew what his allowances added up to. He had already worked out that a 20% rise on base was his floor, and that a move before the gratuity date would cost him a specific amount he could quote to the dollar. We spent the rest of the call on whether a new employer could make up that gap, either through a higher base or through some other part of the package, which is a far more useful conversation than starting from a vague percentage.

Most people I speak to are less exact about the percentage, though in my experience Hong Kong candidates know their bonus release date well. Those who plan to move either wait until the bonus lands or ask the new employer to make up the difference through a sign-on payment or a higher base. The ones who struggle are those who have not put a figure on what they would be giving up, so they cannot tell whether an offer actually covers it.

Candidates in data and AI have the strongest position right now, and hiring managers know it. If you have competing conversations, say so early, because it changes how a manager prices the role. If you are asking for well above the usual range, be ready to show what you bring that justifies it, whether that is production experience, a specific stack, or a team you have led.

I would also encourage you to walk in with a view on which parts of the package you would trade and which you would not. Sign-on payments are not standard, so do not build your plan around one. A manager with a fixed base budget may have some room elsewhere, though, and finding out what that is before the offer arrives lets you steer the conversation instead of reacting to the first number.

In 2013, I applied for an internship at a small agency and got a generic no.

So I did what career advice still tells you to do. I wrote back and asked for feedback: what could I do better, and how should I keep refining my search?

This was the reply (attached):

"As a small agency, we cannot take time to help you and the many, many folks that request help."

I did everything right and still heard that I was one of too many. I had graduated without a job lined up, I was working catering gigs, and I was looking for any way into HR.

I kept that email. Last week I showed it to students at Texas A&M SHRM Chapter. 

They're walking into a tighter version of that market. A Stanford study found employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs fell about 13% since late 2022. Still many, many folks asking for help.

I'm back in the search myself right now, and here's what's working for me:

1. Ask for feedback anyway. Most people won't answer. The few who do make it worth it.

2. Brief before every conversation. I use AI to research the company and the person first, so I show up with better questions. AI does the research. You do the relationship.

3. Sit at more than one table. Communities post internships, contract roles, and referrals before job boards do.

4. Follow up within 48 hours, and track it. Most people don't, which is why it works.

Thank you, Texas A&M SHRM and Sasha Golovine and Sarah Lubin for coordinating.

To anyone hiring entry-level HR talent: those rooms are full of people worth your time.

Anthropic just published a study of how AI changed work inside their own company, and it is the clearest picture we have seen of where the rest of us are heading.

They studied their own staff: hiring records, output numbers, calendars, Slack, agent logs, and 17 interviews. The main findings are these:

1. By August, AI agents were working six hours for every one hour a person worked.
2. Engineers ship five times more code than six months ago. Lawyers process more contracts, sales reps close more deals, finance clears more invoices.
3. The share of junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9% in about 18 months.
4. People now spend about a fifth of their AI sessions on "meta-work": writing instructions for agents, building dashboards to watch them, and getting one agent to check another.
5. Hiring managers care less about domain expertise and more about judgment and autonomy, because the AI does the execution.
6. The bottleneck is now human attention. Reading everything the agents produce would take a non-technical employee more than half the working week.

Two things from this apply directly to companies here in the Philippines.

First, the productivity jump did not come from buying a tool. It came from people rebuilding their own work around it, one repeated task at a time. A sales rep built their own pipeline dashboard in an afternoon. A finance manager built an agent to review purchase requests. Nobody waited for IT.

When AI compresses a 40-person project into a 2-person team, is it a blessing or a curse?

Aaron Levy, CEO and co-founder of Box, recently shared a sharp perspective that every founder and business leader needs to hear: As AI makes building easier, competition is actually becoming more brutal.

Having taken Box from a college dorm to a public company across multiple tech eras, Aaron highlights three critical truths we often overlook:

1. "MVP Inflation": Building is cheaper, but advantages are vanishing

We saw a startup recently run by just two people—something Aaron noted would have required at least 40 people five years ago. But here is the catch: Your competitors’ teams have also shrunk from 40 to 2.

 * 10x development efficiency doesn’t mean your market advantage expands 10x, because the entire market just got the same upgrade.

 * In the past, "being able to build the product" was a defensive moat. Today, it’s merely an entry ticket. A demo is no longer a finished product; it's just a digital draft.

2. Don't be fooled by Coding Agents: Real enterprise adoption is slower than expected

The explosive success of coding assistants has led many to assume sales, legal, finance, and HR will automate overnight. But coding is an outlier—it’s digital-native, highly structured, and provides instant feedback loops with self-debugging.

Real-world enterprise work involves something entirely different: trust, budgets, legacy systems, compliance, risk, and human organizational habits. "Generatable" does not equal "automatable." AI diffusion into real enterprises will face more friction than Silicon Valley expects.

3. The Great Migration: From "Building Intelligence" to "Driving Adoption"

As frontier models become more powerful, raw "intelligence" is rapidly depreciating in value. Where does profit migrate?

It moves to the messy, non-standardized layers: deep industry context, legacy integrations, strict compliance, workflow restructuring, and most importantly—Adoption.

The hardest part of entrepreneurship is shifting from "Can you build it?" to "Can you get it embedded into daily workflows?"

Looking Ahead: From Chat to Background Agents
Aaron predicts that in five years, 90% of corporate tokens won't be triggered by humans typing prompts in a chat window. Agents will autonomously scan contracts, process data, execute workflows in the background, and only surface items when human approval is required.

The Bottom Line:

AI can save you from hiring 38 people, but it does the exact same favor for your 38 competitors.
The defining question of the AI era is no longer "Can we build this?"

It is: "When everyone can build it, why will it be us?"
